newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to trim low-wage job subsidy - paper.
newsitem.headline: France to trim low-wage job subsidy - paper.

text.p: The French government has decided to cut back a subsidy for low wage jobs in order to save about 10 billion francs ($1.6 billion) and give it some much-needed financial breathing room, the daily Liberation reported on Saturday.

The savings, which Liberation said would go to new jobs creation programmes, would help Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin keep a central campaign promise that a plan to create 150,000 youth jobs in the public sector next year would be paid for by reorganising extensive state job subsidies and not by new spending.

The paper reported the decision the day after Jospin put the finishing touches to ministry spending levels for 1998, wrapping up one side of a budget that is crucial to France's preparations for European monetary union.
Jospin's office refused to comment on the report and no one at the Finance Ministry was available for comment.

Jospin was seeking savings to allow the country to cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) to qualify for the planned single European currency but still boost employment and the economy.

An audit of public finances released on July 21 showed France on track for a deficit of 3.5 to 3.7 percent of GDP without corrective action. On the same day, the government announced savings to trim the deficit by around 0.4 percent of GDP.
The jobs plan, which promises to create a total of 350,000 youth jobs in the public sector over the next few years, is expected to cost the government about 10 billion francs in 1998.

The paper said Jospin decided to trim the subsidy over the objections of Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn and Employment Minister Martine Aubry, who were reported to believe that cutting the cost of labour to employers was the best way to boost employment.

The paper reported without citing any sources that a sliding scale exoneration from payroll charges applied to jobs that pay up to 1.33 times the minimum wage would be lowered, and also altered so it would not apply if employers are already benefitting from another subsidy. ($ = 6.218 French Francs)
